uses.text: About 85 % of potash (potassium salts) is sold as fertiliser.
The rest goes into chemical and industrial uses.
Potassium hydroxide makes soaps and detergents; potassium chloride is a salt substitute; a sodium–potassium alloy carries heat in some reactors.

Causes severe skin burns and eye damage

Stack height 13 px. LOW PRECISION: the model abundance is small on this box's scale, so 1 px = 0.08 of the total. Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.' Paper: 'K, Sc, V and Ti are known to be under-produced at all metallicity ranges in theoretical models with respect to the observations' and 'The under-production of the elements around Ti is a long-standing problem.'

air.text: Tarnishes at once; oxidises so fast that the metal can melt and ignite.

water.text: Reacts violently with water, giving potassium hydroxide and hydrogen, which ignites with a lilac flame.

plantRole.text: The main cation of the cell sap; drives turgor and stomatal opening and activates many enzymes, without being built into organic molecules.

humanRole.text: The main positive ion inside cells; with sodium it sets the membrane potential of nerves and muscles.

roles.text: The main positive ion inside cells, needed for nerves and muscles to work.
In baker's yeast it balances the negative charges in the cell and is needed to make proteins.
The most common singly charged positive ion inside the cell: E. coli holds about 0.3 mol per litre.
One of the major positive ions of prokaryotic cells, though how much a cell holds varies widely between species.
Halobacteria balance the salty water outside by holding potassium chloride at molar concentrations inside, and their proteins are built to work in it.

history.nameOrigin: Named by Davy after potash ('pot ashes'), the alkali he electrolysed to obtain it.
history.symbolNote: K comes from the New Latin kalium, from the Arabic al-qali, 'plant ashes'.
history.note: The first metal ever obtained by electrolysis, from molten caustic potash.

prose.text: Potassium is a soft alkali metal that reacts so violently with water that the hydrogen released catches fire, its flame tinted lilac by the potassium. Living things depend on it: plants use potassium to open and close the pores in their leaves, which is why potash is a major fertiliser, and our nerves rely on it too. A small fraction, 0.0117 %, of natural potassium is radioactive potassium-40, with a half-life of about 1.25 billion years, so every human body is faintly radioactive. The nineteenth electron enters 4s rather than 3d, giving [Ar] 4s¹ (ground term ²S₁/₂): the first place in the table where a new shell starts before the one beneath is full.
